_about: Each entry puts one known bug back into internal/web and the suite must fail. The set is weighted toward the security decisions rather than the plumbing: a mutant that survives on the CSRF layer or the certificate store means the test suite does not actually pin the control it claims to. Run: python3 scripts/mutate.py scripts/mutations/web.json

the CSRF comparison leaks timing on a secret. The mutant adds `got == want ||` in front of the constant-time compare. The two
expressions return the same bool for every possible pair of inputs, so no test can
distinguish them: the only difference is how long the comparison takes, and timing
is not an observable a unit test in this package has.

Marking it equivalent is a claim, so it is checkable: delete the `got == want ||`
prefix and every test in internal/web still passes -- in particular
TestAPostWithoutACSRFTokenIsRefusedAndDoesNothing,
TestAPostWithTheSessionsTokenIsAccepted and
TestAnotherSessionsCSRFTokenIsNotAccepted, which together pin that a correct token
is accepted, a missing one is refused, and another session's token is refused. All
three go through this comparison, so they pin that it exists and is reached; none of
them can pin that it is constant-time.

What the mutant is really guarding against -- someone swapping the constant-time
compare for a plain == -- is therefore a review property, not a test property.

This is the exact regression the branch's own 'not wired into this build' notice existed to catch, and a notice is not a test. Widened to cover the assembly when serveEngine extracted the field assignments -- deleting `engine.Run,` alone left the variable unused, so the mutant had become a build failure rather than a bug.

the guard counts constructed backends instead of usable ones -- the exact defect a review caught. Names() lists what the registry could build, and a constructor only fails on a nil runner or an unknown id, so this fires on a typo in lockBackends and stays silent on a machine where loginctl exists and exits 1. The daemon then announces that enforcement is running, serves the admin UI, and can lock nobody. Written as the regression rather than as a generic weakening, so the battery keeps guarding the specific mistake

the audit pre-flight removed: the writer opens lazily, so an unwritable trail surfaces as the first dropped event hours later instead of as a startup failure the operator who can fix it is standing in front of

the startup line sent nowhere. This is the guard whose absence broke CI and not the author's desktop: it is the only stdout write that does not depend on a lock backend answering the probe, so TestTheTLSSWarningIsNotOnStdout's premise -- that stdout carries something before the warning -- was quietly a fact about the machine. A daemon whose log records only exceptions does not say it came up, and does not say which config it opened, which is the one mistake that reads as success

the availability report is printed but never counted, so usable stays 0 and a machine that can lock somebody is refused at startup. This is the direction the guard could be 'fixed' in to look safe: refusing always passes every refusal test, so the control -- a usable backend must start -- is what this mutant needs, and TestServeStartsWhenOneBackendIsUsable is what kills it

Every form then reads as missing its token -- but the point is the reverse direction: a guard that ties the check to the shared constant follows the field when it is renamed, and one that hard-codes a string keeps checking a name that no longer exists while reporting full coverage.

the reach check matches the template's own action text against the rendered action. A template action is a Go template expression (/users/{{$who}}/override) and a rendered action is a URL (/users/casey/override), so the two never match and every templated form is reported as markup no page renders. The {{...}} to * folding is the whole mechanism, so it gets a mutant.

the liveness check inverted. Reading a registration out of the source is not the same as the router having it: this comparison is what makes 'the scanner read a string' mean 'the server answers that route', and without it a registration behind a branch that never runs would be counted as covered.

the premise of a source-based route guard inverted. extraRoutes is a real second way onto the router and it is written, by either spelling, only in tests today, which is the only reason reading the source is enough; the moment a production caller sets it, this guard is coverage theatre and needs a different mechanism. Inverted, it reports that fact on the current tree and stays silent on the tree where it matters.

the composite-literal half of the field scan never collects. This is the reviewer's demonstration: `&Server{extraRoutes: f}` writes the field and is not a statement, so a scan that reads only AssignStmts reports the field as test-only while production sets it in a constructor, and the guard that licenses the whole route scan says so with a clear conscience. The synthetic case for this shape is the only thing that can catch it, because extraRoutes is written by neither spelling outside the tests today.

an untyped composite literal is guessed 'not a Server'. That is the inner element of `[]*Server{{extraRoutes: f}}`, where the type is implied by the enclosing literal and the node alone does not say what it builds. Guessing is the quiet answer again; the cost of guessing the other way is a loud failure naming a file.

the literal's TYPE stops being checked and any struct literal with a same-named field counts as a write. Caught by the guard's own negative control, which is the only case that can see it: a scan that reports everything passes every positive assertion in the file, exactly as a scan that reports nothing does.

Caught by the real dashboard rendering and by the hand-built joined cell in TestTheLockoutCheckRejectsAJoinedCell.

the positional comparison stops comparing: every non-empty label is accepted, so a cell labelled with a neighbouring column's name passes again. The rule was membership before and that is what let the copied label through, which is why the hand-built bad table in TestTheLabelCheckRejectsAHandBuiltTable is what catches this -- no real page in the suite contains a wrong label, so no page test can.

the page list is hand-written again, which is the state that let the audit page ship unvisited while the guard claimed to cover the admin. Caught by the count, not by any per-page assertion: three pages pass every check, and only "four pages had a cell checked" notices the fourth is gone.

mutants.old:
complaints = append(complaints,
			path+" renders a rows table with no ordinary cells, so nothing was checked")
mutants.note: a table that prints its headers and no rows stops being reported. This is the vacuity half of the guard: without it an empty fixture reads as a clean page, and the same deletion applied to a page test would silently drop that page from coverage. Caught by the empty-table case in TestTheLabelCheckRejectsAHandBuiltTable.

the rule is narrowed to the one string the old template happened to produce, so it stops being a rule about joins and becomes a match against a fossil: any other word glued to the state ("locked outnow", a future countdown) passes. Caught by the hand-built joined cell, which is written as markup rather than as that string.

the rule answers "the name is fine" for every filter, so a typo keeps its closed, confident answer and the note never renders. TestTheRuleForWhenANoteIsOwed pins the predicate directly; TestATypoedAccountIsNamedAsATypo pins the sentence the operator reads.

rows on screen stop mattering, so a deleted account's own events are contradicted by the existence note. TestTheRuleForWhenANoteIsOwed's "filter matched, name not in the listing" case; the page-level version of this survived a battery until the predicate was extracted, because audit.tmpl renders the note only inside its filtered-empty branch and masked the handler's copy of the condition. The len(rows) > 0 clause is DEFENSIVE, not reachable: the only caller guards len(rows) == 0 before calling, so this mutant is caught by the predicate test alone and no request can drive it. Stated because a reader who assumes it is reachable will go looking for a caller that does not exist.

a listing that answered nothing becomes an empty account set, which is the one reading of a failed read that is definitely wrong. TestTheRuleForWhenANoteIsOwed's "the listing did not answer" case, and TestAnUnansweredListingKeepsThePageSilentAboutExistence at the page.

the account listing is opened on every filtered request, including the ones that already found the account, so a listing that fails can reach an answer it was never asked for. TestTheListingIsReadOnlyWhenTheFilterFoundNothing counts the seam calls in both directions, because a mutant that deletes the read entirely has to fail the other half.

the existence check stops requiring the name to be present, so any listing at all says the typed name exists. TestACaseVariantIsRefusedAndExplainedRatherThanMatched, which is also the proof the fix did not loosen the match: Linux names are case-sensitive and Mallory and mallory can be two children.

the failure direction inverted: a listing that answered is logged as though it failed and a listing that failed falls through to the branch that answers from it. TestATypoedAccountIsNamedAsATypo loses the sentence and TestAFailedAccountListingIsLoggedWhenTheNoteIsWithheld loses both halves at once. Re-pointed in #94's review round -- the handler used to read `if listing, lerr := s.readAccounts(); lerr == nil {`, and the reason line the reviewer asked for moved the error out of the condition.

mutants.old: There is no account named {{.User}} among the accounts plock can manage on this machine right now
mutants.new: There is no local account named {{.User}} on this machine right now
mutants.note: the sentence goes back to asserting what accounts exist on the machine, which is the over-claim #94 exists to close and the finding that reopened it: users.List is filtered by uid range and login shell and drops both in silence, so `useradd -u 900` is a real child the listing has never seen. TestTheNoteNamesTheFilterThatSaidNoRatherThanTheMachine fails on both its halves -- the managed-set wording and the pinned absence of the old claim.

the narrowed sentence stays but stops naming the filter that answered no, which leaves the operator with a black box and no way to notice the filter is the wrong one. TestTheNoteNamesTheFilterThatSaidNoRatherThanTheMachine's `uid 500-1500` assertion.

the guard on the range is dropped, so a listing that carries no bounds renders `uid 0-0` -- a number the page made up, and the zero value is the one value that must never read as a fact here. TestAListingWithoutBoundsInventsNoRange.

the bounds are carried through in the wrong order, so the page reports a range that was never applied (and one that reads as inverted). Both variables stay read, which is why the mutant swaps rather than zeroes: `= 0` orphans uidMin and the battery would print a build failure as a catch. TestTheNoteNamesTheFilterThatSaidNoRatherThanTheMachine.

a refused account listing is swallowed without a trace, which is the failure the reviewer named: the page's contract is that silence is a verdict, and a page that chose not to speak is then indistinguishable in the log from one that could not look. The trail's failed read two screens up logs for the same reason. `&& false` keeps lerr read so the mutant compiles. TestAFailedAccountListingIsLoggedWhenTheNoteIsWithheld.

every filtered-empty request is logged as a refused listing, including the ones that answered. The control half of W161: without it a handler that logs unconditionally passes the log assertion. It also stops computing the note at all, so the typo test fails with it. TestAFailedAccountListingIsLoggedWhenTheNoteIsWithheld's control.

mutants.old: out = append(out, formOnPage{action: action, shape: formShape(block[1]), hasToken: tokenField.MatchString(block[1])})
mutants.new:
_ = tokenField
		out = append(out, formOnPage{action: action, shape: formShape(block[1]), hasToken: true})
mutants.note: The token detector reports every form as carrying the field, whatever the markup says. No page can then fail the property, and the guard's own control catches it: TestTheFormDetectorNoticesWhatItClaimsToSee feeds markup whose token field is renamed and requires it to read as unprotected. This mutant is why that control exists -- every other page in the suite is a page that is currently correct, so without it the guard could pass because it stopped noticing.

formShape returns the empty string, so every form reports the same identity and the two arms of a conditional cell vouch for each other again -- the regression this change exists to close. Killed twice: TestTheFormDetectorNoticesWhatItClaimsToSee requires the two arms' shapes to differ, and TestEveryFormOnEveryPageCarriesTheToken's reach check can no longer tie a defined form to a served one. sort.Strings is repeated in `new` only to keep the import referenced; a mutant that fails to build is invalid, not caught.

mutants.old: served[f.shape] = servedWhere{action: f.action, where: "state " + state.name + " on " + p}
mutants.new: served[f.action] = servedWhere{action: f.action, where: "state " + state.name + " on " + p}
mutants.note: Reach keyed back on the action instead of the form's shape: the exact pre-fix behaviour, where a cell posting both arms of one conditional to one URL lets the rendered arm satisfy the reach check for the arm no fixture ever renders. TestEveryFormOnEveryPageCarriesTheToken fails because no defined form's shape is ever found among the served keys.

a server assembled without the lock seam answers "0 of 1 locked" instead of saying the daemon is the broken half. The refusal is also what keeps the page from reading the table and reporting an empty result for a daemon that never asked. TestAServerWithNoLockPathSaysSo.

a typo'd name walks on to the listing, finds nothing, and is answered "has no session on this machine" -- the audit page's dead end arriving through the write path, where the operator then believes the child is logged out. TestLockingAnUnmanagedAccountIsRefused.

an account with no session renders a result page with no rows and a summary of "locked 0, unconfirmed 0, refused 0", which reads as a failed lock rather than as an account that is not logged in. TestAnAccountWithNoSessionSaysSo.

mutants.old: s.pageError(w, r, "the session table could not be read", err)
mutants.new: s.pageRefuse(w, r, http.StatusConflict, name+" has no session on this machine")
mutants.note: the exact lie the guard exists to prevent: a listing that could not be read is rendered as a confident statement that the child has no session. The seam is the one that shells out to loginctl, so it fails on a real machine. TestAFailedSessionListingIsNotReportedAsNoSession.

the page stops saying this account is the one the daemon runs inside, so the operator sees "locked" next to an account the schedule will never hold (#67) and believes the machine is protected. TestLockingTheDaemonsOwnAccountSaysBothHalves.

mutants.old: name, res.Locked, res.Unconfirmed, res.Refused, sessionName(s, r)))
mutants.note: the audit line claims a lock on every request whatever the chain answered, so the trail an operator reads afterwards is the page's optimism rather than the machine's record. TestALockRequestIsAuditedWithCountsNotAVerdict.

the dashboard keeps saying a schedule will never hold the account and stops offering the one action that locks it now -- the half of the sentence that was the complaint. Only the button goes, so the page still parses: the mutant is the missing control, not a broken template. TestTheDashboardOffersToLockAManagedAccount.

an unwired probe seam renders a table with no rows in it, which an operator reads as 'every backend is broken' when what is broken is this daemon's wiring. The refusal is the only honest answer for a nil seam, and it is the answer the assembled-wrong case exists to catch. TestAServerWithNoProbePathSaysSo.

the banner reports zero reachable backends however many actually answer, so a machine with a working backend is shown as having none and the operator goes hunting for a fault that is not there. TestEachBackendIsReportedWithItsOwnAnswer.

a session table that could not be read is reported as an account with no session. The two sentences look alike and mean opposite things: one is 'nobody is logged in', the other is 'the daemon could not look', and the second is the one that needs fixing. TestAFailedSessionListingStillReportsTheBackends.

the probe stops writing the line the operator's own action is supposed to produce, so the trail shows a check being asked for that the record never mentions -- and the trail is the evidence read back afterwards. TestAProbeIsAuditedWithCountsNotAVerdict.

every session is reported as one a lock would be attempted on, including the greeter and the remote session the enforcement loop declines. The page explains a refusal the loop would not make, which is a second, contradicting account of one rule. TestANonLockableSessionIsRefusedInTheLoopsOwnWords.

the route answers for any name in the URL, so the probe page becomes a way to ask about an account this daemon does not manage. The same guard is what makes the lock route refuse, and a page beside it cannot be exempt. TestProbingAnUnmanagedAccountIsRefused.

the dashboard keeps the row's explanation and drops the control, so the probe is a route nothing links to and no operator will ever press -- the #59 failure, where a feature shipped assembled and unreachable. Only the button goes, so the page still parses: the mutant is the missing control, not a broken template. TestTheDashboardOffersToCheckTheBackends.

the unconfirmed verdict wearing the locked colour. The word still says unconfirmed, so an assertion on the word passes while the cell is styled as a proved lock -- and the colour is what the eye reads before the sentence. The sibling page already guards its own version of this. TestAnUnconfirmedLockIsReportedAsUnconfirmed.

a refused session wearing the locked colour. This is the row that means the child is still at their screen, and --held is the class the page reserves for a proved lock; the word in the cell still says not locked, so an assertion on the word passes. TestARefusedLockNamesTheSessionItCouldNotReach.

the banner drops the "and that is every session" half of its condition, so proving one of two sessions prints "casey is locked" over a page whose second row says the backend refused. The sentence an operator quotes to a child. TestAPartialProofIsNotPrintedAsTheWholeAccountIsLocked.

the refused cell saying locked next to the backend's own refusal. W187 pinned this cell's class and left its word free, and the only other grep near the row matches the banner's sentence, not the cell. TestARefusedLockNamesTheSessionItCouldNotReach.

the flag paragraph claiming 'those were proved' on a page where nothing was proved. One comparison holds the sentence back, so deleting the condition makes the page assert proved locks that do not exist. TestAnUnconfirmedLockIsReportedAsUnconfirmed.

mutants.old: name, res.Locked, res.Unconfirmed, res.Refused, sessionName(s, r))
mutants.note: the audit trail folding refused sessions into the locked count. A greeter row is refused before any backend is asked, so the trail records a lock no backend ever saw -- on the surface an operator reads afterwards as evidence. TestALockRequestIsAuditedWithCountsNotAVerdict.

the self-session note printed on every row. Its last clause is 'you asked for this one, so it happened', so on a refused row the page claims a lock happened. TestLockingTheDaemonsOwnAccountSaysBothHalves.
